source:
Ridership on the Harbor Line fell eleven percent last year, the steepest drop since the line opened, and the two officials responsible for it cannot agree on why.

Transit director Ingrid Halvorsen says the answer is the schedule. In March the agency cut evening frequency from every ten minutes to every twenty to cover a driver shortage. "People do not plan their lives around a train that might come," Halvorsen said at Tuesday's board meeting. "When we went to twenty minutes after seven, the evening riders left, and they did not come back when we restored the tens in September." The agency's own counts show evening boardings down twenty-six percent, against a daytime decline of four percent.

Councilmember Rafael Ibarra, who chairs the transportation committee, reads the same numbers differently. The fare rose from two dollars to two seventy-five in February, a month before the schedule change. "The director keeps pointing at the timetable because the timetable was her decision to make," Ibarra said. "The fare increase was the council's, and it hit exactly the riders who have a choice. Evening riders are the discretionary trips. Raise the price and the discretionary trips are the first to go." Ibarra noted that the neighboring Valley Line, which kept its ten-minute evening service, still lost seven percent of its evening riders after the same fare increase.

Halvorsen does not dispute the Valley Line figure but says it cuts the other way. "Valley lost seven with no schedule change. We lost twenty-six with one. The gap between seven and twenty-six is the schedule." Ibarra responds that the Valley Line serves a wealthier corridor where a seventy-five-cent increase matters less, so the two lines cannot be compared rider for rider.

Both agree that the restored September schedule has not brought evening riders back, and both agree the agency should not raise fares again this year. Where they part is what to do next. Halvorsen wants a six-month guarantee of ten-minute evening service, advertised heavily, to rebuild the habit. Ibarra wants a fare rollback to two twenty-five on evening trips, which he says would test his explanation directly.

The board will take up both proposals in November. An agency analyst who asked not to be named said the two effects were hard to separate because they happened within weeks of each other, and that the agency has no rider survey from the period.

extraction.mainQuestion: What caused the eleven percent drop in Harbor Line ridership last year?

positions.thesis: Cutting evening frequency from ten to twenty minutes caused the ridership loss, because unreliable evening service made riders abandon the train.
positions.steelman: Evening boardings fell twenty-six percent while daytime fell only four, and the line that kept ten-minute evening service lost far less; the gap is the schedule.

caveats: The reporter presents both officials without taking a side and is not assigned a position. The unnamed analyst is quoted but not treated as a participant. Ibarra's remark about why the director favors the timetable explanation is his own assertion and is not adopted by this analysis.
